nodes.label: Training Needs Analysis
nodes.one_line: Tell whether a performance gap is actually a training problem before a budget gets spent building training for it.
know_what: Performance gap — the measurable difference between what people currently do and what the organization needs them to do
Front-end analysis (Rossett) — the assessment package (job, task, organizational, and gap analysis) done before deciding on a solution
Non-training solutions — job aids, incentive redesign, tool changes, staffing changes that fix a gap training can't touch
Mager & Pipe's flowchart — a diagnostic sequence asking 'could they do it if their life depended on it?' to separate skill deficits from everything else
Business impact vs. learning impact — the distinction between what the organization needs to see change and what a learner needs to be able to do
Sponsor's presenting problem — the framing a sponsor arrives with, which is often the symptom, not the cause
know_how: Interview the sponsor for the presenting problem, then ask for the data behind it (metrics, complaints, error rates) before agreeing training is the fix
Apply Mager & Pipe's could-they-do-it-if-their-life-depended-on-it test to separate a skill deficit from a motivation or environment problem
Draft a one-page problem statement naming the current state, desired state, and the gap in observable terms
Identify at least one plausible non-training intervention for every training request, and rule it out explicitly rather than silently
Estimate the cost of doing nothing against the cost of a training solution before recommending one
Document the decision (train / don't train / hybrid) with the evidence that drove it, so it survives a later 'why did we build this'
habits: Ask 'what would you see them doing differently' before asking 'what do you want them to know'
Treat the first request as a hypothesis, not a spec
Default to suspicion of any request that names a solution before naming a problem
Look for the metric that already exists before proposing a new one
Assume some of the gap is non-training and go looking for which part

know_why.claim: A full front-end analysis should precede every training request, even a small one.
know_why.because: skipping it produces training built for the wrong gap, which costs more in production rework than the analysis would have taken
know_why.disputed_by: rapid/agile instructional design practitioners, who argue a lightweight one-page problem statement plus a fast prototype finds the same information cheaper than a formal analysis phase
know_why.source: Rossett's front-end analysis framework vs. Michael Allen's Successive Approximation Model (SAM)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a stakeholder's request for a training solution, produce a one-page analysis that names the performance gap, rules out at least one non-training cause, and states a go/no-go recommendation with evidence.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting the sponsor's requested solution (a course) as the deliverable spec instead of treating it as a hypothesis about the cause, then building training that doesn't move the metric the sponsor actually cared about.
sources: Robert Mager & Peter Pipe, Analyzing Performance Problems
Allison Rossett, front-end analysis framework
Thomas Gilbert, Human Competence (Behavior Engineering Model)

nodes.label: Writing Measurable Learning Objectives
nodes.one_line: Write an objective specific enough that two different people would agree on whether a learner met it.
know_what: ABCD format — Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree; the four slots a fully specified objective fills
Mager's three-part objective — performance, condition, criterion, a simpler ancestor of ABCD
Verb bank — observable-behavior verbs (identify, calculate, troubleshoot) versus banned verbs (understand, know, appreciate) that can't be observed
Terminal vs. enabling objective — the one big objective a module builds toward versus the smaller objectives that support it
Condition statement — the tools, references, or constraints available when the behavior is performed ('given a live ticketing queue', 'without notes')
Criterion — the standard that separates passing from failing performance (accuracy percentage, time limit, error tolerance)
know_how: Rewrite a topic ('participants will learn about de-escalation') as a behavior with a condition and criterion
Run every draft objective through the verb bank and flag any objective using an unobservable verb
Separate a module's terminal objective from its enabling objectives and check the enabling set is sufficient to reach the terminal one
Set a criterion using existing performance data (current error rate, current time-to-completion) rather than an arbitrary round number
Check an objective is assessable by drafting the assessment item for it on the spot; if you can't write the item, the objective isn't specific enough
Cut objectives that don't trace back to the diagnosed gap, even if they're 'nice to know'
habits: Read a draft objective and ask 'what would the test question for this look like' before accepting it
Flag 'understand' and 'know' on sight
Ask whether an objective is terminal or enabling before deciding how much time it gets
Push back on objectives added because they're easy to teach rather than because they close the gap
Keep a running check: a module with a full page of objectives usually isn't chunked yet

know_why.claim: Every objective should specify an observable behavior, banning verbs like 'understand' or 'appreciate.'
know_why.because: an unobservable objective can't be assessed, so the course has no way to prove it worked
know_why.disputed_by: constructivist and andragogy-leaning designers, who argue behavioral objectives flatten open-ended or dispositional goals (like 'develop a habit of reflection') into things that were never meant to be checklist-measurable
know_why.source: Robert Mager, Preparing Instructional Objectives, vs. Elliot Eisner's critique of behavioral objectives

nodes.checkpoint: Given a training request and a diagnosed gap, write a terminal objective and at least two enabling objectives in full ABCD form, each one you could draft an assessment item for on the spot.
nodes.common_failure: Writing an objective that names the topic ('participants will learn about the new CRM') instead of the behavior, which then makes every downstream assessment and activity decision unmoored.
sources: Robert Mager, Preparing Instructional Objectives
Bloom's Taxonomy, revised edition (Anderson & Krathwohl)
ABCD framework (Heinich, Molenda, Russell & Smaldino)

nodes.label: Instructional Strategy Selection
nodes.one_line: Pick direct instruction, worked examples, PBL, or simulation based on the objective's cognitive demand and the learner's novice/expert level, not habit.
know_what: Direct instruction — explicit, instructor-led explanation and demonstration, strongest for novices and procedural or factual objectives
Worked-example effect — showing a fully solved problem outperforms unsupported problem-solving for novices (Sweller)
Problem-based learning (PBL) — presenting an authentic ill-structured problem before instruction, strongest for advanced learners with prior knowledge to draw on
Expertise reversal effect — a strategy that helps a novice (heavy guidance) can hurt an expert, since redundant guidance competes with their existing schema
Simulation / scenario-based learning — practicing a decision in a consequence-bearing but safe environment, strongest for judgment-heavy objectives
4C/ID model (van Merriënboer) — whole tasks first, part-task practice second, for complex professional skills
know_how: Match a strategy to the objective's cognitive demand: procedural or recall objectives to direct instruction, judgment or troubleshooting objectives to scenario or PBL
Check the audience's prior-knowledge level before choosing between heavy-guidance and minimal-guidance approaches
Default to worked examples plus faded guidance for a genuinely novice audience, regardless of how sophisticated the objective looks
Switch strategy mid-curriculum as learners move from novice to intermediate, instead of running one strategy the whole course
Justify a strategy choice in writing against the objective and audience so a reviewer can trace the decision
Pilot a contested strategy choice on a small group before committing a full production budget to it
habits: Ask what the learner already knows before deciding how much guidance to give them
Resist the default of 'let's make it a simulation' when the objective is actually recall or basic procedure
Distrust a strategy chosen because it's trendy or because the SME happens to prefer it
Reconsider the strategy choice whenever the audience profile turns out to be wrong
Write the justification down before defending it out loud, so the reasoning outlives the meeting

know_why.claim: Minimally guided instructional approaches (pure discovery, unguided PBL) are less effective than explicit direct instruction for novices.
know_why.because: novices lack the schema to structure an unguided problem, so working memory is spent on search instead of on the material to be learned
know_why.disputed_by: PBL and discovery-learning researchers, who argue well-scaffolded (not unguided) problem-based approaches outperform direct instruction on transfer and motivation measures, and that the minimal-guidance critique conflates 'minimal guidance' with 'no guidance'
know_why.source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006), 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work', vs. Hmelo-Silver, Duncan & Chinn's response

nodes.checkpoint: Given three objectives at different cognitive levels and an audience profile, select and justify a distinct instructional strategy for each, naming the guidance level appropriate to that audience's prior knowledge.
nodes.common_failure: Picking one instructional strategy for a whole course because it's the designer's favorite or the client's expectation, then bending every objective to fit it instead of matching strategy to objective.
sources: John Sweller, Cognitive Load Theory
Jeroen van Merriënboer, Ten Steps to Complex Learning (4C/ID)
Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006)

nodes.label: Assessment Blueprint Construction
nodes.one_line: Produce a test blueprint that maps every item to an objective, so nothing on the assessment is untaught and nothing taught goes unmeasured.
know_what: Test blueprint / table of specifications — a grid mapping every objective to item count, item type, and cognitive level
Item-to-objective ratio — the rule of thumb (often 3-5 items per objective for a stable score) that keeps a single item from deciding pass or fail
Weighting by objective importance — allocating more items to terminal objectives than to minor enabling ones
Item type selection — matching selected-response, constructed-response, or performance-based items to what the objective actually requires
Cut score — the score that separates pass from fail, set by a defensible method (Angoff, bookmark) rather than a round number
Blueprint review — checking the finished blueprint against the objective list for orphaned objectives (untested) and orphaned items (untraceable)
know_how: Build a grid with one row per objective and columns for item count, item type, and Bloom level
Allocate item counts by objective importance and cognitive complexity, not evenly across the list
Trace every planned item back to a specific objective before a single item gets written
Set a cut score using a stated method and document the rationale, not a default 70 or 80 percent
Flag any objective with zero items and any item with no objective before sign-off
Route the finished blueprint through an SME review pass focused only on coverage, not wording
habits: Build the blueprint before writing a single item, every time, even under deadline pressure
Ask 'what objective does this item test' before accepting any item into the pool
Distrust a blueprint where every objective got exactly the same number of items
Re-check the blueprint against the objectives list whenever an objective changes late
Treat an untestable objective as a signal to go back and rewrite the objective, not the blueprint
nodes.checkpoint: Given a set of 8-10 learning objectives, produce a test blueprint that allocates item counts and types to each objective by importance, with zero orphaned objectives and zero orphaned items.
nodes.common_failure: Writing items first because they're easier to brainstorm than to plan, then reverse-engineering a blueprint to match — which hides objectives no item actually tests.
sources: Robert Linn & Norman Gronlund, Measurement and Assessment in Teaching
Angoff method for standard setting
James Popham, Classroom Assessment: What Teachers Need to Know

nodes.label: Storyboarding & Build
nodes.one_line: Turn a course blueprint into built, sequenced material — storyboard first, then production — without losing the objective-to-content trace.
know_what: Storyboard — a screen-by-screen or scene-by-scene document specifying on-screen text, media, narration, and interaction before production starts
Content-to-objective trace — a column or tag on every storyboard frame linking it back to the objective it serves
Production pass order — script/storyboard, then asset gathering, then build, then media integration, then QA, in that order to avoid rework
Placeholder discipline — marking unfinished assets clearly (for example [PLACEHOLDER: SME video]) so a draft never gets mistaken for final
Version control for builds — naming and archiving storyboard and build versions so a stakeholder's 'go back to the last one' is actually possible
Localization/reuse tagging — marking which frames are likely to need translation or reuse in another course, before build, not after
know_how: Draft a storyboard frame by frame with on-screen text, narration, and interaction spelled out before opening the authoring tool
Tag every frame with the objective ID it serves, and flag any objective from the blueprint with zero frames
Sequence production so scripting and SME review finish before asset production starts, to avoid rebuilding finished assets
Run a storyboard review with the SME and sponsor before build, since revising a storyboard is cheap and revising a built course is not
Build in the authoring tool in the same order as the storyboard, checking off frames as they're completed
Keep a running list of open placeholders and chase each one to a named owner and date
habits: Refuse to open the authoring tool until the storyboard has been reviewed
Ask 'which objective is this frame for' on every frame that doesn't obviously trace back to one
Batch similar production tasks (all narration recording, all screenshot capture) instead of building screen by screen
Flag scope creep the moment a stakeholder asks for a new frame mid-build instead of absorbing it silently
Keep the storyboard as the single source of truth and update it when the build diverges, instead of letting the build silently drift ahead

know_why.claim: A full storyboard should be reviewed and signed off before any build work starts in the authoring tool.
know_why.because: revising a storyboard costs a redline; revising a built interactive screen costs a rebuild, so catching problems early is far cheaper
know_why.disputed_by: rapid-prototyping practitioners (the SAM model), who argue a low-fidelity storyboard hides problems that only show up once something is clickable, and prefer building a rough working prototype early even at the cost of some rework
know_why.source: traditional ADDIE storyboard-first workflow vs. Michael Allen's Successive Approximation Model (SAM)

nodes.checkpoint: Produce a reviewed storyboard for one module where every frame traces to an objective from the blueprint, then build it in the authoring tool with zero unresolved placeholders at hand-off.
nodes.common_failure: Skipping the storyboard and building directly in the authoring tool, which feels faster until a stakeholder wants a structural change deep into production and the whole build has to be re-sequenced.
sources: Michael Allen, Leaving ADDIE for SAM
Cathy Moore, Action Mapping
Articulate Storyline / Rise production workflow documentation

nodes.label: Facilitation Plan Design
nodes.one_line: Write a facilitator's guide detailed enough that someone other than the designer could run the session and hit the same objectives.
know_what: Facilitator's guide — the document specifying timing, talking points, materials, and contingency moves for every segment of a session
Run-of-show — a minute-by-minute schedule that keeps a live session on time without the facilitator watching a clock constantly
Contingency branch — a pre-planned alternate move for when an activity runs short, runs long, or falls flat
Materials checklist — everything a facilitator, including one who isn't the designer, needs staged before the session starts
Co-facilitation handoff points — planned moments where a second facilitator takes over, so a handoff doesn't look improvised
Facilitator notes vs. participant materials — content meant only for the person running the session, kept separate from what learners see
know_how: Build a run-of-show with timing for every segment, padded for the slowest realistic version of each activity
Write contingency moves for the two or three activities most likely to run short or fall flat
Draft facilitator talking points as prompts and cues, not a script to be read verbatim
Stage a materials checklist a facilitator can run through five minutes before the session starts
Pilot the plan with a facilitator who wasn't involved in designing it, and revise based on where they got stuck
Separate facilitator-only notes from participant-facing materials clearly enough that the wrong version never gets projected
habits: Time every segment against a real run-through, not a guess
Ask 'what does the facilitator do if this activity dies' before finalizing a segment
Write for a facilitator who is not you and has never seen this material before
Revisit the plan after every live run and log what actually happened against what was planned
Separate what must happen from what would be nice, so a rushed facilitator still hits the objectives
nodes.checkpoint: Hand a completed facilitation plan to a facilitator who has never seen the course, and have them run the session hitting the stated objectives within 10% of the planned time, using only the plan and materials checklist.
nodes.common_failure: Writing a facilitator's guide only the designer can actually run, because the timing and contingencies exist in the designer's head and never made it onto the page.
sources: Sam Kaner, Facilitator's Guide to Participatory Decision-Making
Cathy Moore, Action Mapping facilitation planning
ATD facilitator guide templates

nodes.label: Piloting & Revision
nodes.one_line: Run a course through one real cohort before full launch, and use what breaks to revise it.
know_what: Pilot cohort — a small, representative group who runs the course before full launch, specifically to surface problems
Pilot vs. beta vs. soft launch — a pilot expects and budgets for major revision; a soft launch expects only minor fixes
Kirkpatrick Level 1/2 pilot data — reaction and immediate learning data collected specifically during the pilot to catch design problems, distinct from ongoing evaluation
Debrief protocol — a structured session with the pilot cohort and facilitator to surface what broke, separate from the survey data
Go / no-go / revise-and-repilot decision — the three real outcomes of a pilot, each with different cost and timeline implications
Revision log — a running record of what changed after the pilot and why, so the next pilot isn't debugging the same issue
know_how: Recruit a pilot cohort that matches the real audience profile, not the most available or most forgiving group
Collect Level 1 and Level 2 data during the pilot using the instruments built for ongoing evaluation, so the pilot doubles as a dry run of the evaluation plan itself
Run a structured debrief with the facilitator immediately after the pilot while the failure points are still fresh
Sort pilot findings into must-fix-before-launch, fix-in-next-revision, and won't-fix, with a stated reason for each
Make an explicit go/no-go/repilot decision and document what evidence drove it
Log every post-pilot change against the specific pilot finding that caused it
habits: Treat every pilot as expected to find real problems, and get suspicious of one that surfaces nothing
Watch the facilitator and the room during a pilot, not just the survey results afterward
Resist the pressure to skip the pilot when the launch date is already public
Ask whether a finding is a content problem, a facilitation problem, or a technical problem before deciding who fixes it
Close the loop with the pilot cohort — tell them what changed because of their feedback

know_why.claim: A course should run through at least one full pilot cohort before general launch, even under deadline pressure.
know_why.because: problems that are invisible on paper — timing, a confusing transition, a broken interaction — only surface when real learners run the actual sequence
know_why.disputed_by: rapid-development practitioners who ship a soft launch to a small live slice of the real audience instead of a separate pilot, arguing a true pilot adds a full cycle of delay for findings a soft launch catches just as well
know_why.source: traditional ADDIE evaluate-before-launch practice vs. Michael Allen's SAM iterative-prototyping approach

nodes.checkpoint: Run a pilot with a representative cohort, collect Level 1/2 data plus a facilitator debrief, and produce a revision log with a go/no-go/repilot decision backed by the evidence collected.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the pilot as a formality to check off rather than a real test — recruiting the easiest group instead of a representative one, then launching regardless of what the pilot found because the date was already announced.
sources: Donald & James Kirkpatrick, Four Levels of Training Evaluation
Michael Allen, Leaving ADDIE for SAM
Robert Brinkerhoff, The Success Case Method
